title: Kubernetes Security
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Kubernetes Security.
Apply kubernetes security to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers kubernetes security in the DevSecOps and Software Supply Chain Security track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Protect pipeline identities and artifacts, pin and review dependencies, keep secrets out of logs, and require human approval for high-impact changes. The specific focus here is kubernetes security; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Kubernetes Security focuses on cluster architecture; kubernetes authentication and authorization; rbac and service accounts. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: Cluster Architecture
items.text: For cluster architecture, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Kubernetes Authentication and Authorization
items.text: Authorization should be enforced for the exact resource and action on the trusted server. Start with least privilege, deny access by default, and test both allowed and denied paths across roles and tenants.

items.title: Admission Controls and Policy Enforcement
items.text: Governance defines accountability and connects requirements to controls, evidence, exceptions, and review cadence. Framework mappings are aids to coverage, not proof of compliance or a substitute for legal interpretation.

items.title: Audit Logs and Runtime Monitoring
items.text: Logs need trustworthy timestamps, useful identity and asset context, retention, access restrictions, and redaction of secrets. A detection rule should have a hypothesis, positive and negative test cases, known blind spots, and an owner.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: DevSecOps makes security verifiable throughout build, review, release, deployment, and maintenance instead of leaving it until the end. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Kubernetes Security. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Cluster Architecture; Kubernetes Authentication and Authorization; RBAC and Service Accounts), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Kubernetes Security is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.
